title: DiffGED: Generative Graph Matching for Graph Edit Distance
one_liner: Instead of predicting one best way to match two graphs, a diffusion model generates many different good matchings at once, so the method avoids getting stuck on bad solutions.
lead: Comparing two graphs by counting how many edits are needed to transform one into the other is a hard problem called graph edit distance. Older methods predict a single best matching between nodes and get trapped in suboptimal solutions. This paper uses a generative model (a diffusion model, one that learns to build things step by step) to produce many different good matchings at once, picking the best result from the diverse set.

paras: Graph edit distance measures how different two graphs are by counting the minimum number of operations (adding or removing edges and nodes) needed to turn one into the other. It is NP-hard, meaning no known algorithm solves it quickly for large graphs.

Recent neural methods speed this up by predicting a single node matching matrix: a grid where each row is a node in the first graph and each column is a node in the second, with high numbers indicating strong matches. Once you have this matrix, you extract the top-k matchings to get candidate edit paths.

The trap: if you predict only one matching, you often land on a local optimum, a bad solution that is hard to escape. Because the candidates are highly correlated (all pulled from the same prediction), you explore similar solutions over and over, missing better paths entirely.

callout.b: Single neural predictions get trapped in bad matchings.
callout.html: DiffGED generates many diverse matchings at once, so you explore a wider space and find better solutions. Because each matching can escape different local traps, at least one of the many candidates is likely to be close to optimal.

steps.text: Cast graph matching as a generation task, not a single prediction.
Start with many random node-matching matrices (noisy states).
Run the diffusion model: iteratively refine all matrices toward valid matchings.
From each refined matrix, pull out the top-k node pairs in one pass, not iteratively.
Compare all candidate paths; return the one with fewest operations.

object.h2: What changes: from single to multiple
paras: Classical neural methods output a single deterministic matrix (one prediction per input). DiffGED generates an entire collection of diverse matching matrices simultaneously. The output shifts from a point estimate to many plausible matchings at once.

hidden.name: diversity metric (spread of candidate matchings)
paras: Diversity measures how different the candidate solutions are from each other. High diversity means you are exploring distant regions of the solution space; low diversity means you are stuck exploring variants of the same bad solution.

DiffGED estimates diversity implicitly by letting the diffusion process run independently on each initial random matrix. If the process is well-calibrated, higher diffusion noise at the start produces more varied final matchings. DiffGED relies on this: starting from random initializations and denoising each in parallel, the model naturally produces a spread of plausible solutions rather than all converging to one.

heat.caption: Darker cells represent more diverse matchings; highlights show strong candidates explored in parallel.

reads.html: Diversity is how different the candidate solutions are. More different candidates explore more of the search space, so you are more likely to find a good solution.
The diffusion generative process produces multiple independent samples from a learned pattern of node matching matrices, increasing diversity compared to deterministic neural predictions.

mechanism.h2: Why generating many matchings avoids traps
paras: A neural network trained to predict a single best matching learns to output what it thinks is the most likely correct answer. On any given input, that prediction will be biased toward high-confidence guesses. If the training data has a common suboptimal local optimum (e.g., a graph pattern that always tricks the model in the same way), the network learns to predict near that trap.

A diffusion model works differently. It learns to denoise: starting from pure noise (random matrices), refine toward any valid matching matrices consistent with the input graphs. Because you start from multiple random seeds, each denoising trajectory can converge to a different local optimum. Some trajectories land in places the deterministic predictor never visits. When you compare all the results, you pick the best one, so even if most land in traps, one is likely to escape.

The second benefit: extracting top-k mappings from a single matrix iteratively (going node by node, each choice constrained by earlier choices) is slow and amplifies mistakes. When you choose the first node-pair, then the second, errors in the first choice propagate to all downstream choices because each choice narrows the remaining options. DiffGED extracts all top-k mappings in one pass from each matrix: instead of choosing sequentially, the model identifies all strong pairs simultaneously, so an error in one pair does not constrain another, and the work completes in a single step instead of k sequential steps.

stages.s: Diffusion model refines each in parallel
Extract one top-k mapping per matrix (no iteration)
Best edit path from diverse candidates

math.words: At each noise-removal step t, the model takes the current noisy matching matrix and the input graphs, then predicts the direction to move to reach a cleaner matrix, scaled by a noise schedule that decreases over time.
math.equation: x_(t-1) = (1/sqrt(alpha_t)) * [x_t - ((1 - alpha_t) / sqrt(1 - bar_alpha_t)) * epsilon_theta(x_t, graphs, t)] + sigma_t * z
symbols: the noisy matching matrix at time step t
the cleaner matrix at the next step
noise schedule value at step t (how much to keep)
cumulative noise from start to step t
neural network that predicts the noise to remove
the scale of random noise added for diversity

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a 3x3 matching matrix at t=10 is completely random, bar_alpha_10 = 0.9.
The model predicts epsilon_theta = [removes 0.4 of the noise].
New matrix x_9 shifts 0.158 * epsilon_theta direction plus fresh Gaussian noise.
After 10 steps, each random seed converges to a different refined matching.
Extract top-k from each; compare all; return the path with fewest edits.

math.note: The diffusion model treats matching matrices like images: it learns to clean up noise step-by-step, starting from many random initializations to produce diverse outputs.

bars.h2: Accuracy and speed compared to existing methods

charts.title: Old deterministic matching
charts.note: Single prediction often misses optimal; extraction is slow.

charts.title: DiffGED (generative)
charts.note: Multiple diverse matchings explore different regions so different seeds escape different local traps; one-pass extraction identifies all pairs at once, not sequentially, so earlier errors do not cascade.

items.html: If the noise schedule (how much noise to add at each step) is not tuned to the graph structure, the denoising may converge to the same solution repeatedly. The model must learn the right amount of noise to maintain diversity.
Running diffusion k times (for k diverse matchings) costs more than a single forward pass. If the graphs are huge, generating many samples may be slower than the speedup from avoiding iteration.

items.b: Quality of the learned graph representation
items.html: Diffusion operates on node matching matrices, which encode the graphs. If the input encoding loses structure, all denoised matrices are unreliable.
DiffGED works best when the noise schedule is calibrated to the data, the graph encoding captures node similarity, and diversity is high enough that at least one sample escapes local optima.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small experiment on two classes of graph pairs: one where a single deterministic prediction gets trapped in a known bad local optimum (e.g., a symmetric graph where naive matching gives low accuracy), and another class where the global optimum is far from the obvious prediction. Run DiffGED and the baseline on both classes. Measure: (1) edit distance accuracy on each class (how close to exact solution), (2) wall-clock time, and (3) how many of the generated candidates are distinctly different from each other (diversity metric).
demo.metric_eq: accuracy = (exact_distance - predicted_distance) / exact_distance * 100; speed = time_diffged / time_baseline; diversity = mean_pairwise_distance_between_candidates
demo.closing: The demo must show that DiffGED's diverse candidates collectively find better solutions than a single prediction, even if some individual candidates are suboptimal. This proves the core idea: because different random seeds lead to different denoising paths, each candidate can escape a different local trap; comparing all candidates reveals one that landed in a better region of the solution space.
